findings.claim: The unit is called Chemistry Paper 1, but L2's second half teaches the Group 0, Group 1 and Group 7 trends and halogen displacement, and the whole of L9 teaches energy changes, reaction profiles, activation energy and bond energies.
findings.truth: Those are topic 6 and topic 7, which the spec assesses on Paper 2. Options: (a) move L9 into the Paper 2 unit and move L2's group-trend sections there too, leaving L2 with Mendeleev, the modern table and electronic configuration (1.13-1.20, common to both papers); or (b) rename the unit if it is meant as a general chemistry unit. The transition-metal collapsible in L2 is 5.1C and does belong on Paper 1.
findings.evidence: spec Paper 1 content: topics 1-5; Paper 2 content: topics 1, 6-9. Topic 6 = Groups in the periodic table; topic 7 = Rates of reaction and energy changes (7.9-7.16 cover exothermic/endothermic, bond energies, activation energy, reaction profiles).

findings.claim: Nine lessons are presented as the Paper 1 unit, but large parts of Paper 1 are never taught.
findings.truth: Missing Paper 1 statements: the whole of topic 2 (2.1-2.12 - states of matter, pure substances and mixtures, separation techniques, paper chromatography and Rf values, potable water) including core practical 2.11; core practical 3.6 (change in pH on adding calcium hydroxide or calcium oxide to dilute hydrochloric acid); 3.12 (tests for hydrogen and carbon dioxide); 3.19-3.21 (solubility rules, predicting precipitates); 4.8 (bacterial and phytoextraction); 4.10-4.12 (recycling, life-cycle assessment); 4.13-4.17 (reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium, Haber conditions 450 degC / 200 atmospheres / iron catalyst, effect of changing conditions). Missing Chemistry-only (C-suffix) Paper 1 statements: 5.16C-5.18C (molar volume 24 dm3 at RTP, Avogadro's law), 5.19C-5.24C (Haber process, fertilisers, ammonium sulfate preparation), 5.25C-5.27C (chemical cells and hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells). 5.1C (transition metals) is only a collapsible aside in L2. Recommend new lessons rather than edits.
findings.evidence: spec topics 2, 3, 4, 5 statement lists; keyword sweep of all nine raw lessons found no occurrence of chromatography, distillation, potable, states of matter, molar volume, 24 dm3, solubility, limewater, fuel cell, fertiliser, life cycle, recycling or phytoextraction, and only one passing mention of the Haber process.

findings.claim: Question 6 is typed '9 marks - Evaluate'.
findings.truth: This paper has no 9-mark items. The longest single item is the 6-mark extended open-response question. Relabelled 6 marks; the band ladder carries no mark numbers, so nothing else changes.
findings.evidence: spec assessment information for Paper 1: 100 marks over ten questions, a mixture of multiple-choice, short answer, calculations and extended open-response.

findings.claim: Question 3 asks students to calculate the relative atomic mass of boron from isotope abundances, with no tier flag, in a lesson tagged tier 'both'.
findings.truth: Calculating Ar from relative masses and abundances is Higher tier only, so the question needs a '(Higher tier)' prefix. The lesson's own content already wraps the matching paragraph in a higher-only block, which is correct and is left alone.
findings.evidence: spec 1.12 is bold in the bold-preserved extraction; 1.11 (explaining why some Ar values are not whole numbers) is not bold and stays open to Foundation.

findings.claim: Question 6 is typed '9 marks - Evaluate'.
findings.truth: Relabelled 6 marks, as F1.
findings.evidence: spec assessment information for Paper 1.

findings.claim: 'Show the word equation or symbol equation for full marks on 3-mark calculation questions about electronic configurations.'
findings.truth: Electronic configuration questions do not ask for equations, and there is no such thing as a 'calculation question about electronic configurations'. Replaced with the actual method: fill the shells 2, then 8, then 8, and check the electrons add up to the atomic number.
findings.evidence: spec 1.19 (predict the electronic configurations of the first 20 elements as diagrams and in the form 2.8.1); the lesson's own worked example uses exactly this method.

findings.claim: 'For magnesium oxide, Mg loses two electrons (2,8 -> 2,8, 0 becomes Mg2+)'
findings.truth: Magnesium has atomic number 12, so its electronic configuration is 2,8,2 and it becomes 2,8 after losing two electrons. The text states the atom's configuration as 2,8 and then produces a stray '0'.
findings.evidence: spec 1.19; L2 of this same unit asks 'What is the electronic configuration of magnesium (atomic number 12)?' and marks 2, 8, 2 correct.

findings.claim: The match check's four left-hand prompts are truncated question stems, e.g. 'ending tells you that an ionic compound contain...' and 'What type of bonding involves the transfer of e...'.
findings.truth: The prompts are cut mid-word, so a student cannot tell what is being asked. Rewritten as short, complete prompts that pair with the existing right-hand answers; the order array is unchanged, so every pairing stays the same.
findings.evidence: the knowledge-check player renders left[i] as the row label and marks the answer against order[i], so the truncation is cosmetic to the data but fatal to the student.

findings.claim: 'students say covalent bonds break when graphite or diamond melts. For graphite, the weak intermolecular forces between layers are overcome on melting, not the covalent bonds - this is why graphite still has a very high melting point.'
findings.truth: This teaches the misconception it claims to correct, and contradicts itself: if only weak forces were overcome, graphite would have a low melting point. Melting diamond or graphite means breaking many strong covalent bonds. The weak forces between graphite layers explain only why graphite is soft and slippery.
findings.evidence: spec 1.32 (giant covalent structures have high melting points because of the covalent bonds throughout the structure), 1.36, 1.37; the lesson's own giant-covalent paragraph states the correct reason.

findings.claim: 'For graphene/fullerenes questions, examiners want the year 1985 (buckminsterfullerene) and 2004 (graphene isolation)'
findings.truth: No date is examinable. The spec asks only for the properties of fullerenes and graphene explained in terms of structure and bonding. Replaced with advice to spend the time on structure and bonding.
findings.evidence: spec 1.38.

findings.claim: Question 6 is typed '9 marks - Evaluate', with bands 'Mastering (7-9)', 'Secure (4-6)', 'Developing (2-3)'.
findings.truth: Relabelled 6 marks and the bands re-cut to 5-6 / 3-4 / 2 / 1, with the internal mark caps reduced so the scheme totals 6.

findings.claim: 'graphite conducts because delocalised electrons move between layers'
findings.truth: The delocalised electron from each carbon moves along its own layer; the lesson's own graphite paragraph says 'free to move along the layers'. Corrected to 'along the layers'.
findings.evidence: spec 1.37; internal inconsistency with the graphite section of the same lesson.

findings.claim: A single higher-only block wraps Limiting Reactants, Percentage Yield and Atom Economy, so Foundation students see none of the three (the CSS rule body.tier-foundation .higher-only sets display:none).
findings.truth: Only the limiting-reactant statement is Higher tier. Percentage yield and atom economy are Chemistry-only statements available at both tiers - this is the 'higher-only used to mean separate-only' build fault. The wrapper is now closed after the limiting-reactant key fact, so percentage yield and atom economy are visible to everyone.
findings.evidence: spec 1.52 is bold (Higher only). 5.11C, 5.12C, 5.13C and 5.14C are not bold. css/style.css line 5062 hides .higher-only for Foundation.

findings.claim: Conversely, the opening sections - the mole, Avogadro's constant, moles = mass / Mr, the two mole worked examples and the mole-ratio section - carry no Higher flag in a lesson tagged tier 'both'.
findings.truth: The mole is Higher tier only in this spec, so Foundation students are shown content they will never be examined on, and the lesson's Foundation view would be thin without it. Options: (a) wrap the two mole sections (n1-n17) in higher-only, keeping the relative-formula-mass paragraph open because Mr is a Foundation statement, which means splitting n3; (b) leave the content open as enrichment and rely on the question-level '(Higher tier)' flags now added in F18; (c) rebuild the lesson as a Foundation reacting-masses lesson plus a Higher mole lesson. I have taken (b) for now because (a) cannot be done without splitting a narration block. Recommend (a) at the next re-narration.
findings.evidence: spec 1.50 and 1.51 are bold (Higher only); 1.43, 1.44, 1.48 and 1.49 are not bold.

findings.claim: The atom-economy formula is given four times with 'sum of Mr of all products' as the denominator, and the exam tip tells students to 'use the Mr values of products only - not reactants'.
findings.truth: The board's definition, and this lesson's own prose definition and glossary entry, use the total Mr of the reactants. The two give the same number for a balanced equation, but a student who writes 'products' in a definition question risks the mark, and the exam tip actively steers them away from the standard method. Changed the denominator to the reactants in the display formula, the key fact, the takeaway, the flashcard, the exam tip and both atom-economy mark schemes.
findings.evidence: spec 5.13C and 5.14C; the lesson's own dfn: 'A measure of how much of the total mass of reactants is converted into useful product'.

findings.claim: The moles exam tip ends: 'In 6-mark describe a method questions on making a salt, examiners explicitly look for: independent variable, dependent variable, control variables, repeats...'
findings.truth: Salt-preparation advice leaked into the quantitative chemistry lesson, and a salt preparation has no independent variable. Replaced with advice that fits the lesson: keep intermediate answers in the calculator and round only at the end.
findings.evidence: spec 3.15-3.18 (salt preparation) sit in L7, not here; the practical is a preparation, not an investigation.

Adding an id changes the block count and needs a re-narration of the lesson, which the brief forbids me from doing here, so it needs Tom's call: add data-narration-id="n33" to the tip and regenerate that one clip.

summary: Every lesson carried at least one finding. The dominant fault is tier mis-wrapping: higher-only blocks hide both-tier Chemistry-only content (percentage yield, atom economy, alloys, electroplating, aqueous discharge rules) from Foundation students, while genuinely Higher-only material (moles, redox by electrons, titration calculations, half equations, bond energies) carries no flag. Beyond that: a wrong magnesium electronic configuration, an exam tip that teaches the graphite melting-point misconception it claims to correct, a match check whose duplicate options mark a correct answer wrong, three 9-mark questions on a paper that has none, leaked salt-practical boilerplate in two lessons, and truncated match prompts in six lessons. Two unit-level items need Tom: L9 (and half of L2) is Paper 2 content, and roughly four lessons' worth of Paper 1 content is missing.
